newsitem.title: GERMANY: Funds expect turnaround soon for German shares.
newsitem.headline: Funds expect turnaround soon for German shares.

text.p: The German share market's dramatic plunge is set to halt as prices hit temptingly low levels and investors start recalling the healthy outlook for corporate earnings, fund managers said on Thursday.

"We are not at all far from the low point now," said Michael Vieker, who manages a 600 million mark ($360 million) German equity fund for Muenchener Kapitalanlage AG and sees good buying chances among auto and chemical stocks.

"Fundamentals here are still the same. The mark is weak compared with most other currencies, which is good news for exporters. And while we have had some increase in long-term interest rates, which is not so healthy, cyclical stocks have a lot of potential."

Panic sparked by Wall Street's sudden sell-off on fears of more interest rate rises has sent Germany's blue-chip DAX index tumbling more than seven percent from a year high and all-time record of 3,474.98 points reached on March 11.
That represents a markedly more dramatic correction than those seen by rivals like Britain's FTSE 100 index.
The DAX dropped 2.62 percent to 3,215.24 points in bourse floor trade on Thursday and dealers were bracing themselves for more losses, describing sentiment as tense and paranoid.

"We might lose another three percent on the DAX but we can see a consolidation coming. There will come a point when investors get their nerve back and start selective buying," predicted Walter Schmidt, managing director of Gerling Asset Management, Cologne, which manages 2.5 billion marks in assets.
Fund managers said the recent price collapse had given breathing space to German shares, whose rapid ascent this year has left many investors suffering a hint of vertigo.

The star among world markets through the spring, the DAX had advanced as much as 20 percent to its highs of early March, levels which beat the most bullish expectations and were widely felt to be somewhat unrealistic.
"If you consider prices were up 50 percent from where we were at the start of 1996, you have to see the logical case to take some profits out," said Vieker.
Estimates for where the DAX will find a floor ranged from 3,180 on the DAX (Vieker) back to 3,100 to 3,120 (Schmidt).

Technical analysts at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett said the DAX had strong technical support at 3,150 points and it "made no sense" to start underweighting Germany now, in the light of the strong earnings trend in export-driven sectors.

"Things will change (on the DAX) and faster than anyone thinks," said Murat Uguz, head of asset management at Frankfurt-based Ceros Asset Management, which manages around 120 million marks in funds and private clients accounts.
"We are still expecting a steady (downward) correction in the medium term but for every 10 percent downward, we see a five percent correction on the upside. We are nearly at that point," Uguz said.

With the German economy on a slow upswing and the dollar holding its own against mark, fund managers are generally putting their faith in companies which are sensitive to the economic cycle and depend on exports.
Schmidt is looking at the car industry in particular, some chemical shares and the steel sector.
Cars are also the tip from Muenchener Kapitalanlage. Non-cyclicals, such as financials, and domestic-driven industries like utilities are expected to generate more modest returns.

But the news is not all good. While Schmidt sees the DAX approaching 3,400 points again by mid-year, he has cut Germany's weighting in his international funds to 40 percent from 50 percent, citing a rapid rise in capital market rates here.
Uguz said his company was negative on equities in general, Germany included, in view of high bond yields.
A U.S. investor, with careful hedging, could expect a 7.5 percent return on a 10-year German Bund without any of the usual stock market risk, he said.
"The logical approach is that you expect a better return for your risk when you buy equities. But this year it is not like that," he said.
-- Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.671 German Marks)
